column6: The commentary has Moses spot a fire and go toward it before the divine address; Exodus places the angel of YHWH in a flame within a bush, making the fire the setting of a call.
The commentary says Moses reaches the fire and is addressed; at the bush God calls “Moses, Moses” and Moses answers, giving the same encounter its direct biblical scene.
The commentary links the fire scene with blessing and glorification; Exodus names the ground around the bush holy and commands Moses to approach reverently, locating sanctity at the fire.

The commentary recalls fires lit as waymarks so people could find and follow a route; Exodus says YHWH led Israel by a pillar of fire at night, an explicit divine fire that lights and guides a journey.

The commentary distinguishes ordinary fire used for warmth from the great punitive fire; Isaiah describes a person using part of his wood fire to warm himself and bake bread, then turns to the religious meaning of the remainder.
The commentary cites roasting meat as one sense of ṣ-l-y; Isaiah's man uses the same fire to roast meat and eat, grounding that sense in an ordinary domestic scene.

The commentary calls the kindled small fire a reminder and contrasts it with turning away from admonition; Isaiah makes the remainder of the cooking fire into an idol that the man bows to, a pointed reversal of fire's proper reminder.

The commentary explicitly reports Arabic nūr and nār together through illumination, while biblical Aramaic uses nūrā for the furnace fire; this supplies a concrete fire-word cognate without proving the commentary's etymology.

The commentary identifies the wretched person as entering the great fire; Isaiah asks who can dwell with consuming fire and everlasting burnings, then answers with the righteous, shifting the question from doomed entry to who can endure God's presence.

The commentary connects Saqar's “does not leave or spare” with the warning that the damned neither die nor live; Isaiah's final image is corpses of rebels with a worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched.

The commentary presents entry into the great fire as punishment for the wretched; Daniel sees the three faithful men walking unharmed inside the furnace with a fourth figure, reversing the expected result of fire-entry.

The Qur'anic Moses scene has blessing and glorification spoken at the fire; after the furnace rescue, Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of the three men, connecting fire, deliverance, and praise in a different scene.

column4: Song of the Three Young Men 3:52-56
column6: The commentary places glorification at Moses' fire and contrasts prayer with damnation; the youths' song blesses and praises God amid the furnace, adding a liturgical voice from inside a fire.
The commentary locates Moses' sighting at the side of Tur; Exodus first brings Moses' flock to Horeb, the mountain of God, grounding the shared fire encounter in its mountain setting.

The commentary quotes the Qur'anic command at the fire to worship and establish prayer; Exodus says Israel will serve God on this mountain after the bush call, linking the encounter to worship while leaving prayer-for-remembrance distinctive to the Qur'anic wording.

The commentary's pious person remembers the Lord's name and prays; at the bush God gives the name by which generations will remember him, making divine name and remembrance part of the same Mosaic scene.

The commentary invokes Moses seeing fire before hearing a call; Stephen recounts the angel appearing in a flame from a bush and introduces Moses' commission, preserving the scene in an early Christian retelling.

The commentary distinguishes the fire verb ṣ-l-y from the prayer verb ṣ-l-w; Daniel's Aramaic verb for his three daily prayers is from the prayer sense, a close Semitic cognate that supports the prayer-side echo without merging the Qur'anic roots.

The commentary contrasts the one who prays with those who say they were not among the prayerful; Daniel keeps praying and thanking God three times daily despite the royal decree, giving a concrete scene of persevering prayer.

The commentary includes roasting meat under Arabic ṣ-l-y; Exodus names the Passover lamb as roasted with fire, a plausible weak-consonant Semitic cognate for that cooking sense, not for the distinct prayer root.
The commentary's person remembers the Lord's name and then prays; the psalm summons the worshipper to bless YHWH and not forget his benefits, joining remembrance to liturgical praise.
The commentary pairs remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer; Jesus' prayer begins by asking that the Father's name be hallowed, a concrete prayer-formula parallel while the verbs differ.
The commentary identifies the wretched one as entering the great fire; the judgment scene assigns the condemned to eternal fire, sharpening the relation between moral fate and fire.

The commentary connects non-ending punishment with fire that does not spare; Jesus applies Isaiah's undying-worm and unquenched-fire language to Gehenna, making the prophetic image an explicit warning about final judgment.

The commentary's damned neither die nor live and the Saqar fire does not relent; Revelation says the smoke of the beast-worshippers' torment rises forever and they have no rest, an analogous account of unending punishment with a distinct image.
The commentary moves from fire at Moses' call to worship and prayer; Hebrews calls God a consuming fire in a passage urging reverent worship, holding judgment-fire and devotion together.

The commentary makes Moses' fire a route to divine address; the midrash reads the thornbush's burning without destruction as God's presence with Israel in affliction, turning the fire into a sign of solidarity and survival.
The commentary joins fire with guidance on a path; Wisdom's retelling says Wisdom guided the holy people and became a starry flame at night, interpreting Israel's fire-guidance as Wisdom's work.
The commentary calls the punishment fire “the great” one; Isaiah describes Topheth's pyre as deep and broad with abundant fire, supplying a concrete biblical scale image for punitive fire.

column5: righteousness as the answer to fire
column6: The commentary contrasts one person entering fire with another remembering God and praying; Isaiah's next verse answers who can dwell by naming the one who acts righteously, offering a specific ethical counterpart to the doomed entrant.

column5: self-kindled fire as light, then torment
column6: The commentary recalls fire used to find a path and contrasts useful fire with the great punishment; Isaiah addresses people who kindle a fire, walk by its light, and end by lying down in torment.

The commentary's Moses hears the divine address at a fire; at Horeb Elijah sees wind, earthquake, and fire, but this verse says YHWH is not in the fire and is encountered in the quiet sound, a distinct counter-scene about revelation.
The commentary treats entry into fire as punishment; after Israel's complaint, YHWH's fire burns at the edge of the camp, giving a concrete wilderness scene of punitive fire.
The commentary contrasts the condemned entrant with the one who remembers God and prays; Moses cries to YHWH and the fire subsides, making prayer an intervention that ends a punitive fire.

column5: Elijah's prayer names God before fire
column6: The commentary pairs remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer; Elijah invokes the God of the ancestors and asks that Israel know YHWH is God before fire answers, joining prayer, divine identity, and fire.

column5: fire descends in answer to prayer
column6: The commentary contrasts going toward a guiding fire with entering a punitive one; after Elijah's prayer, fire falls from YHWH and consumes the offering, reversing the human direction toward fire into a divine response.
The commentary's Moses scene ends in worship and prayer at a fire; after the fire on Carmel, the people fall on their faces and confess YHWH as God, giving a distinct fire-to-worship sequence.

The commentary contrasts the wretched who enter the great fire with the pious kept from it; in Hebrew-numbered Malachi, the coming day burns the arrogant and evildoers like an oven, leaving no root or branch.

column5: he name-fearing spared from the burning day
column6: The commentary pairs remembering the Lord's name and prayer with safety from fire; the next Hebrew-numbered verse promises healing to those who fear God's name, setting their fate against the wicked burned in 3:19.
The commentary glosses al-kubrā through Arabic k-b-r as greatness; Job calls God kabîr, “mighty,” a possible same-root cognate that applies the scale-word to God rather than to a punitive fire.

The commentary develops a fire as a road-marker and links it to being guided; the psalm calls God's word a lamp for the feet and light for the path, pairing illumination with guidance without requiring a shared fire scene.

column5: fire recalled in communal prayer as guidance
column6: The commentary joins fire as a way-sign to remembrance and prayer; Nehemiah's communal confession addresses God while recalling the pillar of fire that lit Israel's path, bringing the same guidance image into a liturgical act.
The commentary stresses the great fire's heat and severity; Nebuchadnezzar orders the furnace heated seven times more than usual, intensifying the furnace image beyond an ordinary flame.

column5: fire kills those who cast the men in
column6: The commentary describes the damned as enduring the fire's heat; Daniel says the furnace's flame kills the men who throw the faithful into it, while the next scene preserves those inside, distinguishing the fire's effects.

The commentary's pious person remembers the Lord's name before prayer; at Moses' fire encounter God gives the self-designation “I am who I am,” adding the name's own explanation to the memorial naming in 3:15.

column5: a sign shown in Moses' call
column6: The commentary cites God's promise to show Moses the greatest signs at the fire; in the continuing bush-call episode Moses' staff becomes a serpent as a sign, giving a concrete counterpart to the signs promised in Qur'an 20:23.

The commentary says the condemned neither die nor live and endure the fire's severity; Luke depicts a dead rich man conscious in flame and asking for relief, adding a specific afterlife image of felt torment.

The commentary presents the great fire as the wretched person's punishment; Hebrews recalls faithful people who quenched the power of fire, giving a Christian counter-example in which fidelity protects from its force.

column5: flaming fire for those who reject the message
column6: The commentary says the wretched turns away from admonition and enters the great fire; Paul describes judgment in flaming fire against those who do not know God or obey the gospel, making the rejection-to-fire sequence explicit.

The commentary records roasting meat under Arabic ṣ-l-y; Exodus uses the Hebrew roasting form for the Passover lamb, a possible cognate for that culinary sense, though the weak final consonants make the relationship uncertain.
